Bequeath

bih-KWEETH · verb

Hear It

What It Means

To bequeath leave or give a thing to someone.

The queen's final decree would bequeath the crown jewels to the national museum rather than to any single heir.

Worked Example

Rather than dividing his farm among his children, the old rancher chose to bequeath the entire property to the local land trust, so it could never be sold off and developed.

Formally arranging, before death, exactly who will receive something afterward is precisely what it means to bequeath it.

How Bequeath Sits Among Its Neighbors

Synonyms — open each to see how it differs

will

will: leave through a legal will

Antonyms

withhold

withhold: deliberately not give

disinherit

disinherit: formally exclude someone from an inheritance

How Strong Is It? — give → bequeath → deed

give vs. bequeath

give vs. bequeath: Give is weaker than bequeath: you can give a friend a book on a whim, while to bequeath something carries the graver weight of a formal gift left in a will.

deed vs. bequeath

deed vs. bequeath: Deed goes further than bequeath: to bequeath property is to promise it through a will someday, while deeding it signs it over permanently, with immediate legal force.

Build the Word

The pieces

Prefix — be-

Prefix — be-: thoroughly (Old English)

Root — queath

Root — queath: to say, to declare (from Old English cwethan, 'to say' -- the same old root buried in bequest and the archaic quoth)

Put it together

Put it together: Bequeath comes from Old English: be- ('thoroughly') + queath (from cwethan, 'to say or declare' -- the same old root buried in the noun bequest). To bequeath something is to formally declare, usually in a will, exactly who should have it.

Use the root in a new word: bequest

Use the root in a new word: bequest: The library's new reading room was funded entirely by a generous bequest from a longtime patron who had passed away that spring.

Root Check

Word Choice

Bequeath specifically means to leave something to someone through a will, after death. Compare endow (earlier in this unit), which means to set up ongoing support, often for an institution, usually while the giver is still alive.
